passages.title: "Houston, We've Had a Problem"
passages.text:
In April 1970, Apollo 13 was on its way to the Moon with three astronauts on board: Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise. It was supposed to be NASA's third Moon landing. Nearly 56 hours after launch, however, one of the spacecraft's oxygen tanks exploded, damaging the main power supply.

"Houston, we've had a problem," Swigert reported calmly to Mission Control. The crew soon realised that the main part of the spacecraft could no longer support them. The Moon landing was cancelled, and the only goal now was to bring the astronauts home alive.

The crew moved into the small lunar module, which had been designed to keep two people alive on the Moon for about two days. Now it had to support three people for almost four days. It became cold, damp and uncomfortable, and the air began to fill with carbon dioxide. On the ground, engineers used only materials that were available on board, including plastic bags, cardboard and tape, to design a device that cleaned the air. The astronauts followed their instructions and built it.

On 17 April 1970, the crew splashed down safely in the Pacific Ocean. Although the mission did not reach its goal, it became known as a "successful failure", because the team had solved a series of problems under enormous pressure.

Today the story is remembered as an example of calm teamwork. The astronauts and the engineers on the ground never stopped working together, even when the situation looked hopeless.
